The Government of Vietnam Proposes a Pilot Visa for Remote Workers

Minister of Culture, Sports and Tourism Lam Thi Phuong Thanh presented a draft resolution on special mechanisms and policies for tourism development to the National Assembly. The draft proposes a controlled pilot program for foreigners working remotely in Vietnam. It also includes more flexible visa and residency conditions for medical tourists and individuals coming for long-term treatment, rehabilitation, or relaxation, along with accompanying family members.

The proposal aims to attract higher-spending tourists and strengthen the competitiveness of the tourism industry. The draft includes the expansion of bilateral visa-free regimes for key markets and a more flexible visa policy prioritizing high-income, long-stay, and repeat visitors, as well as conference participants. The government also proposes simplifying the issuance of work permits, visas, and temporary residence for foreign experts and artists involved in tourism projects.

The pilot program for remote workers has not yet been adopted. The Culture and Social Affairs Committee of the National Assembly, while assessing the project, noted that the resolution should not establish specific visa rules for separate groups and called for further clarification on the novelty, features, and boundaries of the proposed special visa policy. Specific rules, fees, and application procedures for the pilot visa have not been established. Remote workers will continue to use the standard electronic visa valid for up to 90 days.

📌 Data Leak Scams: Why Your Wallet Company Will Never Call You

Main Points
⏺ When a shop or service leaks customer data, scammers get your name, phone and address
⏺ They then call or write pretending to be "support" from your wallet brand
⏺ This post explains how these scams work and how to shut them down in one sentence



1️⃣ Core Idea — A leaked order list tells scammers exactly who owns a crypto wallet. That makes their fake "security alert" sound real. A reseller connected to Trezor recently reported a breach of roughly 27,000 orders.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — The leak doesn't touch your coins. It gives criminals your contact details, so the attack moves from your device to your trust.
3️⃣ Example — You get a call: "Your wallet was compromised, read us your recovery phrase so we can secure it." The caller knows your name and what you bought.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — Phone calls, SMS, emails with "urgent firmware updates", and even paper letters with a QR code to a fake site.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — No real wallet company will ever call you or ask for your seed phrase. Hang up, ignore the link, and only use the official app or website you type in yourself.
Final Thoughts

A data leak is a warning, not a theft. Your funds are safe as long as the seed phrase never leaves your hands — and nobody who asks for it is on your side.

Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections – The White House

Key changes from Executive Order 14248 (Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections) that strengthen election security and fairness:

🔴 Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship (passport, REAL ID, military ID, or equivalent) on the national mail voter registration form
🔴 Gives states free access to federal citizenship, immigration, and Social Security databases to verify voter eligibility and clean rolls
🔴 Directs federal agencies to stop providing voter registration forms without first assessing citizenship
🔴 Prioritizes prosecution of non-citizens who register or vote, and increases coordination with state attorneys general
🔴 Enforces the federal Election Day deadline — no counting of mail/absentee ballots received after Election Day in federal races
🔴 Updates voting system standards to require voter-verifiable paper records and generally prohibit barcode/QR-code-only ballots
🔴 Conditions certain federal election funding on states complying with citizenship proof and ballot-receipt deadline rules
🔴 Restricts non-citizens from accessing election equipment or administering federal elections
🔴 Strengthens enforcement against foreign nationals making contributions or expenditures in U.S. elections
🔴 Improves information-sharing between states and the Department of Justice on suspected election fraud and ineligible voting

These measures aim to ensure only eligible citizens vote, ballots are properly received and verified, and systems produce a clear, auditable paper trail.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.

🪙 A PENNY FROM HIS LUNCH CHANGE SOLD FOR $204,000

In 1947, 16-year-old Don Lutes Jr. of Pittsfield, Massachusetts, noticed something odd in the change from his high school cafeteria: a 1943 Lincoln cent that was copper-colored instead of silvery.

In 1943 the U.S. Mint made pennies from zinc-coated steel to save copper for World War II. A few leftover bronze blanks were caught in the bins that fed the presses and were struck by mistake. Lutes wrote to the Treasury, which told him copper pennies were not struck in 1943. He kept the coin anyway.

Only 10 to 15 examples of the 1943 bronze cent are known, according to Heritage Auctions. On January 10, 2019, Lutes’ coin sold at Heritage in Orlando for $204,000.
